danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 20
paragraphs: Nogle få nære venner spiste som sædvanlig til middag hos Rostoverne den søndag.
Pierre kom tidligt for at finde dem alene.
Han var blevet så tyk dette år, at han ville have set unormal ud, hvis han ikke havde været så høj, så bredskuldret og så stærk, at han bar sin krop med tydelig lethed.

Han gik op ad trappen pustende og mumlende noget. Hans kusk spurgte ikke engang, om han skulle vente. Han vidste, at når hans herre var hos Rostoverne, blev han til midnat. Rostovernes lakaj skyndte sig ivrigt frem for at hjælpe ham af med kappen og tage hans hat og stok. Pierre lod som altid — af klubvane — både hat og stok blive i forstuen.

Den første, han så i huset, var Natasja. Allerede inden han så hende, mens han tog kappen af, hørte han hende. Hun øvede toneskalaer i musikværelset. Han vidste, at hun ikke havde sunget siden sin sygdom, og lyden af hendes stemme overraskede og glædede ham. Han åbnede døren forsigtigt og så hende i den lilla kjole, hun havde båret i kirken, gå rundt i værelset og synge. Hun stod med ryggen til ham, da han åbnede døren, men da hun hurtigt vendte sig og så hans brede, overraskede ansigt, rødmede hun og kom hastigt hen til ham.
"Jeg ville prøve at synge igen," sagde hun og tilføjede, som for at undskylde sig: "Det er i det mindste noget at tage sig til."
"Udmærket!"

"Hvor jeg er glad for, at du er kommet! Jeg er så lykkelig i dag," sagde hun med den gamle livfuldhed, Pierre ikke havde set hos hende i lang tid. "Ved du, at Nikolaj har fået Sankt Georgskorset? Jeg er så stolt af ham."
"Ja, det var mig, der sendte den meddelelse. Men jeg vil ikke forstyrre dig," tilføjede han og ville gå ind i dagligstuen.
Natasja stoppede ham.
"Greve, er det forkert af mig at synge?" sagde hun rødmende og fæstede sit spørgende blik på ham.
"Nej ... Hvorfor skulle det være det? Tværtimod ... Men hvorfor spørger du mig?"

"Det ved jeg ikke selv," svarede Natasja hurtigt, "men jeg ville nødig gøre noget, du ikke billigede. Jeg tror fuldt og fast på dig. Du aner ikke, hvor vigtig du er for mig, hvor meget du har gjort for mig ..." Hun talte hurtigt og lagde ikke mærke til, at Pierre rødmede ved hendes ord. "Jeg så i den samme hærordre, at han, Bolkonskij" — hun hviskede navnet hastigt — "er i Rusland og igen tjener i hæren. Hvad tror du?" — hun talte hastigt, tydeligvis bange for at kræfterne ville svigte hende — "Vil han nogen sinde tilgive mig? Vil han ikke altid bære på en bitter følelse over for mig? Hvad tror du? Hvad tror du?"
"Jeg tror ..." svarede Pierre, "at han ikke har noget at tilgive ... Hvis jeg var i hans sted ..."

Ved denne tankeassociation blev Pierre øjeblikkeligt ført tilbage til den dag, da han havde forsøgt at trøste hende og sagt, at hvis han ikke var sig selv, men den bedste mand i verden og fri, ville han på sine knæ bede om hendes hånd; og den samme følelse af medlidenhed, ømhed og kærlighed greb ham, og de samme ord steg til hans læber. Men hun gav ham ikke tid til at sige dem.

"Ja, du ... du ..." sagde hun og udtalte ordet du med henrykkelse — "det er noget helt andet. Jeg kender ingen venligere, mere generøs eller bedre end dig; det kunne ingen være! Havde du ikke været der dengang — og nu også — ved jeg ikke, hvad der ville være blevet af mig, for ..."
Tårer steg pludselig op i hendes øjne, hun vendte sig bort, løftede noderne op foran øjnene, begyndte at synge igen og begyndte atter at gå op og ned i værelset.
I det øjeblik kom Petja (den yngste Rostov-søn) løbende ind fra dagligstuen.

Petja var nu en smuk, rosenkindet dreng på femten med fyldige røde læber, der lignede Natasja. Han forberedte sig til at begynde på universitetet, men han og hans ven Obolenski havde for nylig i hemmelighed aftalt at gå ind i husarerne.
Petja var stormet ud for at tale med sin navnefælle om denne sag. Han havde bedt Pierre finde ud af, om han ville blive optaget hos husarerne.
Pierre gik op og ned i dagligstuen uden at lytte til, hvad Petja sagde.
Petja trak ham i armen for at fange hans opmærksomhed.
"Nå, hvad med min plan? Pjotr Kirilytj, for Guds skyld! Du er mit eneste håb," sagde Petja.
"Nå ja, din plan. At gå ind i husarerne? Jeg skal nævne det, jeg tager det hele op i dag."
"Nå, mon cher, har du manifestet med?" spurgte den gamle greve (grev Ilja Rostov). "Grevinden har været til messe hos Razumovskijerne og hørt den nye bøn. Hun siger, den er meget smuk."
"Ja, jeg har det," sagde Pierre. "Kejseren kommer i morgen ... der skal være et ekstraordinært adelsmøde, og der tales om en udskrivning af ti mand per tusind. Ja, lad mig lykønske jer!"
"Ja, ja, Gud ske lov! Nå, og hvad nyt fra hæren?"
"Vi trækker os atter tilbage. De siger, vi allerede er nær Smolensk," svarede Pierre.
"Å Herre, å Herre!" udbrød greven. "Hvor er manifestet?"
"Kejserens appel? Nå ja!"

Pierre begyndte at lede i sine lommer efter papirerne, men kunne ikke finde dem. Han blev ved med at klappe på lommerne, kyssede hånden på grevinden, der trådte ind i værelset, og så sig uroligt omkring — tydeligvis ventede han Natasja, der var holdt op med at synge, men endnu ikke var kommet ind i dagligstuen.
"Jeg kan ved min ære ikke finde dem," sagde han.
"Der har vi det, han mister altid alting!" bemærkede grevinden.

Natasja kom ind med et blødgjort og bevæget ansigtsudtryk og satte sig tavst og så på Pierre. Så snart hun trådte ind, lyste Pierres ansigt, der havde været mørkt, pludselig op, og mens han stadig ledte efter papirerne, kastede han flere blikke på hende.
"Nej, virkelig! Jeg kører hjem, jeg må have glemt dem der. Helt bestemt ..."
"Men så kommer du for sent til middag."
"Nåh! Og min kusk er kørt."
Men Sonja, der var gået ud for at lede efter papirerne i forstuen, havde fundet dem i Pierres hat, hvor han omhyggeligt havde stukket dem under foret. Pierre var ved at begynde at læse op.
"Nej, efter middag," sagde den gamle greve, der tydeligvis forventede stor fornøjelse af oplæsningen.

Til middag, hvor der blev drukket champagne for den nye Sankt Georgsridders sundhed, fortalte Sjinsjin dem nyhederne fra byen — om den gamle georgiske prinsesses sygdom, om Métiviers forsvinden fra Moskva, og om hvordan en eller anden tysker var blevet bragt for Rostoptjin, anklaget for at være en fransk "spiån" (sådan havde grev Rostoptjin fortalt historien), og hvordan Rostoptjin havde ladet ham gå og forsikret folk om, at han "slet ikke var en spion, men bare en gammel tysk ruin."
"Folk bliver arresteret ..." sagde greven. "Jeg har sagt til grevinden, at hun ikke bør tale så meget fransk. Det er ikke tiden til det nu."
"Og har I hørt det?" spurgte Sjinsjin. "Fyrst Golitsyn har ansat en lærer til at undervise ham i russisk. Det er ved at blive farligt at tale fransk på gaderne."
"Og hvad med Dem, grev Pjotr Kirilytj? Hvis de indkalder militsen, må De også til hest," bemærkede den gamle greve henvendt til Pierre.
Pierre havde været tavs og adspredt gennem hele middagen og syntes ikke at opfatte, hvad der blev sagt. Han så på greven.

"Ja, krigen," sagde han. "Nej! Hvad for en kriger ville jeg gøre? Og dog er alt så mærkeligt, så mærkeligt! Jeg kan ikke finde hoved og hale i det. Jeg ved det ikke — jeg er langt fra at have militære tilbøjeligheder, men i disse tider kan ingen stå inde for sig selv."
Efter middagen satte greven sig bekvemt til rette i en lænestol og bad med alvorlig mine Sonja, der ansås for en fortræffelig oplæser, om at læse appellen højt.
"Til Moskva, vores ældgamle hovedstad!
"Fjenden har overskredet Ruslands grænser med vældige styrker. Han kommer for at plyndre vort elskede fædreland."
Sonja læste omhyggeligt med sin høje stemme. Greven lyttede med lukkede øjne og gav af og til et brat suk ved visse passager.
Natasja sad rank og rettede sit søgende blik snart mod sin far, snart mod Pierre.

Pierre mærkede hendes øjne på sig og forsøgte at lade være med at se sig om. Grevinden rystede misbilligende og vredt på hovedet ved hvert højtideligt udtryk i manifestet. I alle disse ord så hun kun, at faren, der truede hendes søn, ikke ville være forbi lige med det første. Sjinsjin sad med et sarkastisk smil på læberne og var tydeligvis parat til at gøre nar af hvad som helst, der gav ham mulighed for det: Sonjas oplæsning, enhver bemærkning fra greven eller selve manifestet, hvis intet bedre påskud bød sig.

Efter oplæsningen af de farer, der truede Rusland, og de forhåbninger, kejseren stillede til Moskva og især til dets berømmelige adel, læste Sonja med et skælv i stemmen — hovedsageligt forårsaget af den opmærksomhed, der blev rettet mod hende — de sidste ord:

"Vi vil selv ikke tøve med at vise os blandt Vort folk i den hovedstad og i andre dele af Vort rige for rådslagning og til ledelse af alle Vore opbud, både dem der nu spærrer fjendens vej, og de nyopstillede, der skal besejre ham, hvor end han viser sig. Måtte den undergang, han håber at bringe over os, falde tilbage over hans eget hoved, og måtte Europa, befriet fra trældom, lovprise Ruslands navn!"

"Ja, det er det!" råbte greven, idet han åbnede sine fugtige øjne og gentagne gange snøftede, som om en skarp lugtesalt var blevet holdt under hans næse; og han tilføjede: "Lad kejseren bare sige ordet, og vi ofrer alt og sparer intet."
Før Sjinsjin nåede at slippe den vittighed ud, han havde parat om grevens patriotisme, sprang Natasja op fra sin plads og løb hen til sin far.
"Sikke en dejlig far, vi har!" råbte hun og kyssede ham, og hun så igen på Pierre med det ubevidste koketteri, der var vendt tilbage med hendes bedre humør.
"Se her! Her har I en patriot!" sagde Sjinsjin.
"Slet ikke en patriot, men simpelthen ..." svarede Natasja med fornærmet mine. "Alt er morsomt for dig, men det er slet ikke en spøg ..."
"En spøg!" faldt greven ind. "Lad ham bare sige ordet, og vi drager alle af sted ... Vi er ikke tyskere!"
"Men lagde du mærke til det — der står 'til rådslagning'?" sagde Pierre.
"Ligemeget hvad det er til ..."
I det øjeblik kom Petja, som ingen skænkede opmærksomhed, hen til sin far med et dybt rødmende ansigt og sagde med sin stemme, der knækkede over, snart dyb, snart skingrende:
"Altså, far, jeg siger dig klart og tydeligt, og mor også — I kan gøre, som I vil, men jeg siger klart og tydeligt, at I må lade mig gå ind i hæren, for jeg kan ikke ... det er alt."
Grevinden så forfærdet op mod himlen, knugede hænderne sammen og vendte sig vredt mod sin mand.
"Det er din snak, der har ført til det!" sagde hun.
Men greven havde allerede fattet sig efter sin ophidselse.
"Nå, nå!" sagde han. "Sikke en stolt kriger! Nej! Vrøvl! Du skal læse."

"Det er ikke vrøvl, far. Fjodor Obolenski er yngre end mig, og han skal også af sted. Og desuden kan jeg slet ikke studere nu, når ..." Petja standsede, blev rød til han svedte, men fik dog ordene ud: "når vort fædreland er i fare."
"Hold op, hold op — vrøvl ..."
"Men du sagde jo selv, at vi ville ofre alt."
"Petja! Ti stille, siger jeg!" råbte greven med et blik på sin hustru, der var blevet bleg og stirrede stift på sin søn.
"Og jeg siger jer — Pjotr Kirilytj her vil også sige jer ..."

"Vrøvl, siger jeg. Din moders mælk er knap nok tørret på dine læber, og du vil i hæren! Nu, nu, siger jeg," og greven rejste sig for at gå ud af stuen med papirerne — formentlig for at genlæse dem på sit værelse, inden han tog en lur.
"Nå, Pjotr Kirilytj, lad os gå ud og ryge en pibe," sagde han.
Pierre var ophidset og ubestemt. Natasjas usædvanligt strålende øjne, der uophørligt gled hen over ham med et mere end hjerteligt blik, havde bragt ham i denne tilstand.
"Nej, jeg tror, jeg tager hjem."
"Hjem? Du havde jo tænkt dig at tilbringe aftenen hos os ... Du kommer jo ikke så tit mere, og min pige dér," sagde greven godmodigt og pegede på Natasja, "lyser jo først op, når du er her."
"Ja, jeg havde glemt det ... Jeg er virkelig nødt til at tage hjem ... forretninger ..." sagde Pierre hastigt.
"Nå, så farvel!" sagde greven og forlod stuen.
"Hvorfor tager du af sted? Hvorfor er du ude af dig selv?" spurgte Natasja og så udfordrende ind i Pierres øjne.
"Fordi jeg elsker dig!" var det, han ville sige, men han sagde det ikke, blev blot rød, til tårerne trængte frem, og slog øjnene ned.
"Fordi det er bedst, at jeg kommer sjældnere ... fordi ... Nej, simpelthen fordi jeg har forretninger ..."
"Hvorfor? Nej, sig mig det!" begyndte Natasja bestemt, men standsede pludselig.
De så på hinanden med forskrækkede og forlegne ansigter. Han forsøgte at smile, men kunne ikke: hans smil udtrykte lidelse, og han kyssede tavst hendes hånd og gik.
Pierre besluttede at holde op med at besøge Rostoverne.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: A few close friends were dining with the Rostovs that day, as usual on Sundays.
Pierre came early so as to find them alone.
He had grown so stout that year that he would have looked abnormal had he not been so tall, so broad-limbed, and so strong that he carried his bulk with obvious ease.

He climbed the stairs, puffing and muttering something. His coachman didn't even ask whether to wait. He knew that when his master was at the Rostovs' he stayed until midnight. The Rostovs' footman rushed eagerly forward to help him off with his cloak and take his hat and stick. Pierre, from his club habit, always left both hat and stick in the front hall.

The first person he saw in the house was Natasha. Even before he saw her, while taking off his cloak, he heard her. She was practicing scales in the music room. He knew she hadn't sung since her illness, and the sound of her voice surprised and delighted him. He opened the door softly and saw her in the lilac dress she had worn at church, walking around the room singing. She had her back to him when he opened the door, but when she turned quickly and saw his broad, surprised face, she blushed and hurried up to him.
"I want to try singing again," she said, adding as if by way of excuse, "it is at least something to do."
"That's wonderful!"
"How glad I am you've come! I'm so happy today," she said, with the old liveliness Pierre hadn't seen in her for a long time. "You know Nicholas got a Saint George's Cross? I'm so proud of him."
"Oh yes, I sent that announcement along. But I don't want to interrupt you," he added, and was about to go to the drawing room.
Natasha stopped him.
"Count, is it wrong of me to sing?" she said, blushing and fixing her eyes searchingly on him.
"No... Why should it be? On the contrary... But why do you ask me?"

"I don't know myself," Natasha answered quickly, "but I wouldn't want to do anything you disapproved of. I trust you completely. You don't know how important you are to me, how much you've done for me..." She spoke rapidly and didn't notice how Pierre flushed at her words. "I saw in that same army order that he—Bolkonsky"—she whispered the name quickly—"is in Russia, and back in the army. What do you think?" She was speaking hurriedly, obviously afraid her composure might fail. "Will he ever forgive me? Won't he always hold bitter feelings toward me? What do you think? What do you think?"
"I think..." Pierre replied, "that he has nothing to forgive.... If I were in his place..."

By association of ideas, Pierre was instantly carried back to the day when, trying to comfort her, he had said that if he were not himself but the best man in the world and free, he would ask on his knees for her hand and her love; and the same feeling of pity, tenderness, and love took hold of him, and the same words rose to his lips. But she didn't give him time to say them.

"Yes, you... you..." she said, uttering the word "you" with rapture. "That's different. I know no one kinder, more generous, or better than you—nobody could be! If you hadn't been there then, and now too, I don't know what would have become of me, because..."
Tears suddenly rose in her eyes. She turned away, lifted her sheet music before her face, and began singing again, pacing back and forth across the room.
Just then Petya came running in from the drawing room.

Petya was now a handsome, rosy-cheeked boy of fifteen with full red lips who looked like Natasha. He was preparing for the university, but he and his friend Obolensky had lately agreed, in secret, to join the hussars.
Petya had come rushing out to talk to his namesake about this plan. He had asked Pierre to find out whether he would be accepted in the hussars.
Pierre walked up and down the drawing room, not listening to what Petya was saying.
Petya pulled him by the arm to get his attention.
"Well, what about my plan? Peter Kirilych, for heaven's sake! You're my only hope," said Petya.
"Oh yes, your plan. To join the hussars? I'll mention it, I'll bring it all up today."
"Well, my dear fellow, have you got the manifesto?" asked the old count. "The countess went to Mass at the Razumovskis' and heard the new prayer. She says it's very moving."

"Yes, I've got it," said Pierre. "The Emperor is to be here tomorrow... there's to be a special meeting of the nobility, and they're talking of a levy of ten men per thousand. Oh yes, let me congratulate you!"
"Yes, yes, thank God! Well, and what's the news from the army?"
"We're retreating again. They say we're already near Smolensk," replied Pierre.
"O Lord, O Lord!" exclaimed the count. "Where's the manifesto?"
"The Emperor's appeal? Oh yes!"

Pierre started feeling in his pockets for the papers but couldn't find them. Still patting his pockets, he kissed the hand of the countess as she entered the room and glanced uneasily around, obviously expecting Natasha, who had stopped singing but hadn't yet come into the drawing room.
"I swear, I don't know what I've done with it," he said.
"There he goes, always losing everything!" remarked the countess.

Natasha came in with a softened, emotional expression on her face and sat down, looking silently at Pierre. As soon as she entered, Pierre's gloomy features suddenly brightened, and while still searching for the papers he glanced at her several times.
"No, honestly! I'll drive home—I must have left them there. I'll definitely..."
"But you'll be late for dinner."
"Oh! And my coachman has gone."
But Sonya, who had gone to look for the papers in the front hall, had found them in Pierre's hat, where he had carefully tucked them under the lining. Pierre was about to start reading.
"No, after dinner," said the old count, clearly looking forward to the reading with great anticipation.

At dinner, where champagne was drunk to the health of the new holder of the Saint George's Cross, Shinshin told them the town news: about the old Georgian princess's illness, about Metivier's disappearance from Moscow, and about how some German had been brought before Rostopchin accused of being a French "spyer" (as Count Rostopchin himself told the story), and how Rostopchin let him go, assuring the crowd that the man was "not a spy at all, but only an old German ruin."
"People are being arrested..." said the count. "I've told the countess she shouldn't speak French so much. It's not the time for it now."
"And have you heard?" Shinshin asked. "Prince Golitsyn has hired a teacher to teach him Russian. It's becoming dangerous to speak French in the streets."
"And what about you, Count Peter Kirilych? If they call up the militia, you'll have to mount a horse too," the old count remarked, turning to Pierre.
Pierre had been silent and preoccupied all through dinner, seeming not to grasp what was being said. He looked at the count.

"Oh yes, the war," he said. "No! What sort of warrior would I make? And yet everything is so strange, so strange! I can't make sense of it. I don't know—I'm very far from having military tastes—but in times like these no one can answer for himself."
After dinner the count settled himself comfortably in an easy chair and with a solemn face asked Sonya, who was considered an excellent reader, to read the appeal.
"To Moscow, our ancient Capital!"
"The enemy has entered the borders of Russia with immense forces. He comes to plunder our beloved country."
Sonya read carefully in her high-pitched voice. The count listened with closed eyes, heaving abrupt sighs at certain passages.
Natasha sat upright, gazing searchingly now at her father and now at Pierre.

Pierre felt her eyes on him and tried not to look around. The countess shook her head disapprovingly and angrily at every solemn expression in the manifesto. In all these words she saw only that the danger threatening her son would not be over soon. Shinshin, with a sarcastic smile on his lips, was clearly preparing to mock anything that gave him the opportunity: Sonya's reading, some remark of the count's, or even the manifesto itself if no better target presented itself.

After reading about the dangers threatening Russia and the hopes the Emperor placed on Moscow and especially on its distinguished nobility, Sonya, her voice quivering—mainly from the attention being paid to her—read the final words:

"We ourselves will not delay to appear among our people in that Capital and in other parts of our realm for consultation, and for the direction of all our levies, both those now barring the enemy's path and those freshly formed to defeat him wherever he may appear. May the ruin he hopes to bring upon us recoil on his own head, and may Europe, delivered from bondage, glorify the name of Russia!"

"Yes, that's it!" cried the count, opening his moist eyes and sniffing repeatedly, as if someone had held strong smelling salts under his nose; and he added, "Let the Emperor just say the word and we'll sacrifice everything and hold nothing back."
Before Shinshin had time to deliver the joke he had prepared about the count's patriotism, Natasha jumped up from her seat and ran to her father.
"What a darling our Papa is!" she cried, kissing him, and she looked at Pierre again with the unconscious flirtatiousness that had returned with her better spirits.
"There! That's a patriot for you!" said Shinshin.
"I'm not a patriot at all, I'm simply..." Natasha replied in a hurt tone. "Everything seems funny to you, but this isn't a joke at all..."
"A joke, he says!" the count put in. "Let the Emperor just say the word and we'll all go... We're not Germans!"
"But did you notice, it says 'for consultation'?" said Pierre.
"Never mind what it says..."
At this moment Petya, to whom nobody was paying any attention, came up to his father with a very flushed face and said in his breaking voice—now deep, now shrill:
"Well, Papa, I'm telling you right now—and Mama too—think what you want, but I say absolutely that you must let me join the army, because I can't... that's all."
The countess, in dismay, looked up at the ceiling, clasped her hands, and turned angrily to her husband.
"This is what comes of your talk!" she said.
But the count had already recovered from his excitement.
"Come, come!" he said. "What a fine warrior you are! No! Nonsense! You have to study."

"It's not nonsense, Papa. Fedya Obolensky is younger than me, and he's going too. Besides, I can't study now when..." Petya stopped short, blushing until he perspired, but still got out the words, "when our Fatherland is in danger."
"That's enough, that's enough—nonsense..."
"But you said yourself we'd sacrifice everything."
"Petya! Be quiet, I tell you!" cried the count, with a glance at his wife, who had turned pale and was staring fixedly at her son.
"And I'm telling you—Peter Kirilych here will tell you too..."

"Nonsense, I tell you. You've barely stopped nursing at your mother's breast and you want to go to war! There, there, enough," and the count started to leave the room with the papers, probably to reread them in his study before having a nap.
"Well, Peter Kirilych, let's go have a smoke," he said.
Pierre was agitated and confused. Natasha's unusually brilliant eyes, continually glancing at him with more than friendly warmth, had put him in this state.
"No, I think I'll go home."

"Home? Why? You were going to spend the evening with us... You don't come often enough as it is, and this girl of mine," said the count good-naturedly, nodding toward Natasha, "only brightens up when you're here."
"Yes, I forgot... I really must go home... business..." said Pierre hurriedly.
"Well then, goodbye!" said the count, and left the room.
"Why are you going? Why are you upset?" asked Natasha, and she looked challengingly into Pierre's eyes.
"Because I love you!" was what he wanted to say, but he didn't say it. He only blushed until the tears came, lowered his eyes.
"Because it's better for me to come less often... because... No, I simply have business..."
"Why? No, tell me!" Natasha began firmly, and suddenly stopped.
They looked at each other with dismayed and embarrassed faces. He tried to smile but couldn't: his smile expressed suffering, and he silently kissed her hand and went out.
Pierre made up his mind not to go to the Rostovs' anymore.
